claim: In classical descriptions of vertebrate development, the segregation of the three embryonic germ layers completes by the end of gastrulation.
source: In classical descriptions of vertebrate development, the segregation of the three embryonic germ layers completes by the end of gastrulation.
evidence: This is a statement about established scientific knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Body formation proceeds in a head to tail fashion by progressive deposition of lineage-committed progenitors during regression of the primitive streak (PS) and tail bud (TB).
source: Body formation then proceeds in a head to tail fashion by progressive deposition of lineage-committed progenitors during regression of the primitive streak (PS) and tail bud (TB).
evidence: This is a statement about classical understanding in developmental biology.

claim: Retrospective clonal analysis identified a population of neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) contributing to both musculoskeletal precursors (paraxial mesoderm) and spinal cord during axis formation.
source: The identification by retrospective clonal analysis of a population of neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) contributing to both musculoskeletal precursors (paraxial mesoderm) and spinal cord during axis formation challenged these notions.
evidence: This refers to previous research findings that identified NMPs.

claim: Classical fate mapping studies of the PS region in amniotes have failed to provide direct evidence for bipotential cells at the single-cell level.
source: However, classical fate mapping studies of the PS region in amniotes have so far failed to provide direct evidence for such bipotential cells at the single-cell level.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research approaches.

claim: A resident cell population of the anterior PS epiblast contributes to neural and mesodermal lineages in trunk and tail in chicken embryos.
source: Here, using lineage tracing and single-cell RNA sequencing in the chicken embryo, we identify a resident cell population of the anterior PS epiblast, which contributes to neural and mesodermal lineages in trunk and tail.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on lineage tracing and scRNAseq experiments.

claim: Cells of the anterior PS epiblast initially behave as monopotent progenitors and only acquire a bipotential fate later, in more posterior regions.
source: These cells initially behave as monopotent progenitors as classically described and only acquire a bipotential fate later, in more posterior regions.
evidence: This is a finding from the lineage tracing experiments described in the study.

claim: NMPs exhibit a conserved transcriptomic signature during axis elongation.
source: We show that NMPs exhibit a conserved transcriptomic signature during axis elongation but lose their epithelial characteristicsin the TB.
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA sequencing analysis presented in the study.

claim: NMPs lose their epithelial characteristics in the tail bud.
source: We show that NMPs exhibit a conserved transcriptomic signature during axis elongation but lose their epithelial characteristicsin the TB.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and gene expression analysis in the study.

claim: Posterior to anterior gradients of convergence speed and ingression along the PS lead to asymmetric exhaustion of PS mesodermal precursor territories.
source: Posterior to anterior gradients of convergence speed and ingression along the PS lead to asymmetric exhaustion of PS mesodermal precursor territories.
evidence: This is based on live imaging and cell tracking experiments described in the study.

claim: Through limited ingression and increased proliferation, NMPs are maintained and amplified as a cell population which constitute the main progenitors in the TB.
source: Through limited ingression and increased proliferation, NMPs are maintained and amplified as a cell population which constitute the main progenitors in the TB.
evidence: This is based on cell tracking, proliferation analysis, and ingression measurements in the study.

claim: At stage 4-5HH, SOX2 expression domain progressively expands posteriorly to reach the anterior PS and the adjacent epiblast.
source: At stage 4- HH (Hamburger and Hamilton, 1992), SOX2 is only expressed in the neural plate in the anterior epiblast and its expression domain progressively expands posteriorly to reach the anterior PS and the adjacent epiblast at stage 4-5HH (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: SOX2 expression levels show a graded pattern, which peaks in the anterior neural plate and decreases in the epiblast lateral to the anterior-most PS.
source: SOX2 expression levels show a graded pattern, which peaks in the anterior neural plate and decreases in the epiblast lateral to the anterior-most PS (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of immunostaining shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: No SOX2 expression is detected in the epiblast adjacent to the posterior PS at stages 4-5HH.
source: No SOX2 expression is detected in the epiblast adjacent to the posterior PS.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining observations.

claim: T expression shows a reverse gradient along the PS, with low levels in the epiblast around the node region and high levels in the posterior end of the PS.
source: At these stages, T expression shows a reverse gradient along the PS, with low levels in the epiblast around the node region and high levels in the posterior end of the PS (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: At stage 4+HH, opposing gradients of SOX2 and T begin to overlap in the epiblast lateral to the anterior PS, defining a SOX2/T territory that forms an inverted V capping the PS.
source: At stage 4+HH, these opposing gradients begin to overlap in the epiblast lateral to the anterior PS, defining a SOX2/T territory that forms an inverted V capping the PS (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is based on double immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C, D and supplementary figures.

claim: At stage 5HH, numerous double-positive SOX2/T cells are found in the epiblast of the anterior PS region, with the underlying mesoderm expressing the paraxial mesoderm-specific marker MSGN1.
source: At stage 5HH, numerous double-positive SOX2/T cells are found in the epiblast of the anterior PS region, with the underlying mesoderm expressing the paraxial mesoderm-specific marker MSGN1 (Figure 1E, F, E', F', levels 2 and 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining of tissue sections shown in Figure 1E, F and supplementary figures.

claim: Posterior to the SOX2/T domain, the epiblast of the PS region expresses T but not SOX2, while the underlying mesoderm maintains a high level of MSGN1 expression.
source: Posterior to this domain, the epiblast of the PS region expresses T but not SOX2, while the underlying mesoderm maintains a high level of MSGN1 expression (Figure 1E, F, E'', F'', level 4).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining of tissue sections shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: In regions of the epiblast corresponding to the prospective intermediate mesoderm/lateral plate and the extraembryonic mesoderm, epiblast cells express T but not SOX2 and no MSGN1-positive cells are found in the underlying mesoderm.
source: Posterior to these two domains, in regions of the epiblast corresponding to the prospective intermediate mesoderm/lateral plate and the extraembryonic mesoderm (Psychoyos and Stern, 1996), epiblast cells express T but not SOX2 and no MSGN1-positive cells are found in the underlying mesoderm (Figure 1E, F, level 5).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E, F and reference to previous fate mapping studies.

claim: The presumptive paraxial mesoderm territory of the epiblast of the anterior PS can be subdivided into an anterior domain where cells co-express SOX2 and T (presumptive NMP territory) and a posterior PMP domain where cells express T but not SOX2.
source: Therefore, the presumptive paraxial mesoderm territory of the epiblast of the anterior PS can be subdivided into an anterior domain where cells co-express SOX2 and T corresponding to the presumptive NMP territory and a posterior PMP domain where cells express T but not SOX2 (Figure 1D, E', E'').
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both the NMP and PMP domains are characterized by the production of MSGN1-positive PMPs.
source: Both domains are characterized by the production of MSGN1-positive PMPs.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data showing MSGN1 expression in the mesoderm underlying both domains.

claim: During PS regression up to the 10–12-somite stage, the SOX2/T cells were maintained in the epiblast lateral to the anterior-most part of the PS, below Hensen's node.
source: During PS regression, that is, up to the 10–12-somite stage, the SOX2/T cells were maintained in the epiblast lateral to the anterior-most part of the PS, below Hensen's node (arrowhead, Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining of embryos at different stages shown in Figure 1G.

claim: After the 10-somite stage, SOX2/T cells were found in continuity with the posterior-most SOX2-positive/T-negative neural tube.
source: After the 10-somite stage, cells were found in continuity with the posterior-most SOX2-positive/T-negative neural tube (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: SOX2/T cells eventually became located in a superficial region of the tail bud at the 25-somite stage where they remain at least until stage 26HH.
source: These SOX2/T cells eventually became located in a superficial region of the tail bud at the 25-somite stage where they remain at least until stage 26HH (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012; Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G and reference to previous work.

claim: At the 25-somite stage, electroporated cells from the SOX2/T region at stage 5HH were found in the neural tube, paraxial mesoderm, and superficial region of the tail bud.
source: At this stage, electroporated cells were found in the neural tube, paraxial mesoderm, and superficial region of the tail bud where the SOX2/T cells were identified (Figure 1G, I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is based on electroporation and live imaging experiments shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: The tail bud territory contains descendants of the SOX2/T cells of the anterior PS epiblast region of stage 5HH embryos.
source: Thus, this tail bud territory contains descendants of the SOX2/T cells of the anterior PS epiblast region of stage 5HH embryos.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electroporation and tracking experiments.

claim: Anterior cells of the SOX2/T territory undergo limited movements along the AP axis and move to join the neural tube.
source: We observed anterior cells undergoing limited movements along the AP axis and moving to join the neural tube (Figure 1J, red tracks, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging and cell tracking shown in Figure 1J and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Cells in the middle of the SOX2/T territory moved in the AP direction but undergo very limited medial to lateral movements and neither joined the neural tube nor the mesoderm.
source: Cells in the middle of the SOX2/T territory moved in the AP direction but undergo very limited medial to lateral movements (Figure 1J, gold tracks, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, Videos 1 and 2). These cells neither joined the neural tube nor the mesoderm, suggesting that they remained in a progenitor state.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging and cell tracking shown in Figure 1J and supplementary figures.

claim: Some posterior cells of the SOX2/T territory undergo dorsal to ventrolateral movements into the mesoderm.
source: In contrast, some posterior cells undergo dorsal to ventrolateral movements into the mesoderm (Figure 1J, green tracks, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging and cell tracking shown in Figure 1J and supplementary figures.

claim: The data supports lineage continuity and conserved bipotential fate of the SOX2/T territory during axis elongation.
source: Therefore, our data supports lineage continuity and conserved bipotential fate of the SOX2/T territory during axis elongation, suggesting that NMPs constitute a stem cell population able to contribute to the neural and mesodermal fates and to self-renew.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cell tracking and fate analysis experiments.

claim: Descendants of bipotent cells from retroviral barcoding were found in both anterior (before somite 27) and posterior regions of the axis.
source: Descendants of bipotent cells were found in both anterior (before somite 27, which marks the transition between primary and secondary neurulation; Le Douarin et al., 1998), and posterior regions of the axis (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the spatial distribution of barcoded cells shown in Figure 2B and reference to previous work.

claim: Using Nucbow lineage tracing, 47 clones containing a total of 690 cells in the neural tube and paraxial mesoderm were identified in six embryos.
source: We identified 47 clones containing a total of 690 cells in the neural tube and paraxial mesoderm in six embryos (Figure 2D–K).
evidence: This is based on Nucbow lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 2D-K.

claim: While both monopotent neural and mesodermal clones were found using Nucbow, the majority of the clones were bipotent.
source: While we found both monopotent neural and mesodermal clones, the majority of the clones were bipotent (Figure 2E–G, J, K).
evidence: This is based on quantification of clone types from Nucbow experiments shown in Figure 2E-G, J, K.

claim: Bipotent clones from Nucbow were found both in the anterior and posterior region, and they often exhibit descendants of only one lineage in some regions and of the other lineage in other regions.
source: Bipotent clones were found both in the anterior and posterior region, and they often exhibit descendants of only one lineage in some regions and of the other lineage in other regions (Figure 2F, K).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the spatial distribution of Nucbow clones shown in Figure 2F, K.

claim: The lineage-tracing analysis provides direct evidence for the existence of bipotent NMP cells located in the SOX2/T region of the anterior PS epiblast in the chicken embryo.
source: Thus, our lineage-tracing analysis provides direct evidence for the existence of bipotent NMP cells located in the SOX2/T region of the anterior PS epiblast in the chicken embryo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the retroviral barcoding and Nucbow lineage tracing experiments.

claim: scRNAseq analysis of the posterior embryonic region during PS to tail bud transition in chicken revealed a distinct NMP cluster lying between a cluster of PSM cells and one of neural cells.
source: scRNAseq analysis of the posterior embryonic region during PS to tail bud transition in chicken and mouse revealed a distinct NMP cluster lying between a cluster of PSM cells and one of neural cells.
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Using diffusion pseudotime and WOT trajectory inference analysis, two developmental trajectories leading from NMPs to neural and PSM clusters were identified, consistent with the bipotentiality of these cells.
source: Using two different trajectory inference analysis methods (diffusion pseudotime and WOT), we identified two developmental trajectories leading from NMPs to these neural and PSM clusters, consistent with the bipotentiality of these cells.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of scRNAseq data using trajectory inference methods.

claim: A signature of genes enriched in the NMP clusters was identified, including a majority of effectors and targets of wnt signaling.
source: From our analysis, we identified a signature of genes enriched in the NMP clusters, including a majority of effectors and targets of wnt signaling, which is known to play a key role in the differentiation of this lineage (Henrique et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data and reference to previous work on Wnt signaling in NMPs.

claim: Most NMP signature genes are expressed in all chicken and mouse NMP clusters.
source: Most of these signature genes are expressed in all chicken and mouse NMP clusters.
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression across NMP clusters in chicken and mouse scRNAseq data.

claim: Using WOT trajectory analysis, cells within the NMP cluster were identified as ancestors of the paraxial mesoderm and neural clusters in the mouse and chicken embryo.
source: Using WOT trajectory analysis, we identified cells within the NMP cluster as ancestors of the paraxial mesoderm and neural clusters in the mouse and chicken embryo.
evidence: This is based on computational trajectory inference analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: No bias for the NMP contribution toward the neural or mesodermal fate was found in the WOT analysis.
source: We were not able to find any bias for the NMP contribution toward the neural or mesodermal fate.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of transition probabilities from WOT analysis.

claim: A developmental trajectory within the NMP cluster was identified using diffusion pseudotime and WOT analyses, suggesting that NMP cells undergo maturation during axis formation.
source: Using diffusion pseudotime and WOT analyses, we also identified a developmental trajectory within the NMP cluster, suggesting that NMP cells undergo maturation during axis formation.
evidence: This is based on trajectory inference analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Clusters of early and late NMPs characterized by expression of specific genes were identified in both chicken and mouse.
source: This is supported by the identification of clusters of early and late NMPs characterized by expression of specific genes in both chicken and mouse.
evidence: This is based on reclustering analysis of NMP cells from scRNAseq data.

claim: Late NMPs are characterized by the expression of more posterior Hox genes in both chicken and mouse.
source: As reported for mouse embryos (Wymeersch et al., 2019), late NMPs are characterized by the expression of more posterior Hox genes in both chicken and mouse.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis of early and late NMP clusters and reference to previous work.

claim: Genes associated to the epithelial state such as EpCAM, CDH1, or GJA1 are downregulated while genes associated to the mesenchymal state are upregulated at tail bud stages in both chicken and mouse.
source: We also observed that genes associated to the epithelial state such as EpCAM, CDH1, or GJA1 are downregulated while genes associated to the mesenchymal state are upregulated at tail bud stages in both species.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis between early and late NMP clusters.

claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis using the epithelial to mesenchymal transition gene set showed a positive enrichment score only for the late NMP clusters in chicken and mouse.
source: To assess globally if NMP early and late cells were undergoing EMT, we performed a Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) using the epithelial to mesenchymal transition gene set (Subramanian et al., 2005). We find a positive enrichment score (NES) only for the late NMP clusters in chicken and mouse, suggesting that NMP cells in the tail bud are undergoing Epithelial to Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) (Figure 5I–L).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5I-L and reference to the GSEA method.

claim: SOX2/T double-positive cells in the epiblast (early NMPs) exhibit strong apical expression of CDH1.
source: Consistent with our single-cell data analysis, we found that SOX2/T double-positive cells in the epiblast (i.e., early NMPs) exhibit strong apical expression of CDH1.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining of tissue sections shown in Figure 5M.

claim: SOX2/T cells in the tail bud (late NMPs) do not express CDH1 while strong expression is detected in the adjacent epithelial ectoderm.
source: In contrast, SOX2/T cells in the tail bud (i.e., late NMPs) do not express CDH1 while strong expression is detected in the adjacent epithelial ectoderm.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining of tissue sections shown in Figure 5N.

claim: During their maturation SOX2/T cells lose their original epithelial characteristics in the tail bud, concomitantly with expression of the more posterior Hox gene paralog groups.
source: This argues that during their maturation SOX2/T cells lose their original epithelial characteristics in the tail bud, concomitantly with expression of the more posterior Hox gene paralog groups.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the immunostaining and gene expression data.

claim: 44 conserved genes between chicken and mouse NMP signatures were found, showing a striking enrichment in Wnt pathway genes.
source: We found 44 conserved genes between the two species showing a striking enrichment in Wnt pathway genes including known targets such as Axin2, T, and Fgf8 as well as pathway members including Wnt3a/5a/5b/8a and Wls.
evidence: This is based on comparison of differentially expressed genes in chicken and mouse NMP clusters.

claim: 38 genes conserved in four or five of the six NMP datasets (chicken, mouse embryos, and human in vitro) were identified.
source: We identified 38 genes conserved in four or five of the six datasets.
evidence: This is based on comparison of NMP signature genes across multiple datasets from different species and studies.

claim: The conserved NMP gene list includes signaling proteins such as Wnt5a, Wnt8a, Fgf17, and Cyp26a1 as well as T and Nkx1.2.
source: This list includes signaling proteins such as Wnt5a, Wnt8a, Fgf17, and Cyp26a1 as well as T and Nkx1.2.
evidence: This is based on analysis of conserved genes across NMP datasets.

claim: The conserved NMP gene list includes glucose transporters (Slc2a3 [glut3] and Slc2a1 [glut1]) and lactate dehydrogenase isoforms (Ldha and Ldhb), consistent with the high level of glycolysis occurring in the tail bud of chicken and mouse embryos.
source: Interestingly, the glucose transporters (Slc2a3 [glut3] and Slc2a1 [glut1]) as well as the lactate dehydrogenase isoforms (Ldha and Ldhb) were also identified in this list consistent with the high level of glycolysis occurring in the tail bud of chicken and mouse embryos (Bulusu et al., 2017; Oginuma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on analysis of conserved genes and reference to previous work on glycolysis in the tail bud.

claim: The conserved NMP gene list includes genes coding for transcription factors such as Cdx1/2/4, Evx1, Hes3, Sp5/8, and Hoxc9.
source: This list also included genes coding for transcription factors such as Cdx1/2/4, Evx1, Hes3, Sp5/8, and Hoxc9.
evidence: This is based on analysis of conserved genes across NMP datasets.

claim: Epiblast cells exhibit a posterior to anterior gradient of convergence speed toward the PS.
source: Thus, epiblast cells exhibit a posterior to anterior gradient of convergence speed toward the PS (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on cell tracking and velocity measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: Posterior cell trajectories are less persistent than anterior ones, indicating that cells in the posterior part of the PS exit the epiblast layer sooner than cells of the anterior region.
source: Posterior cell trajectories are less persistent than anterior ones, indicating that cells in the posterior part of the PS exit the epiblast layer sooner than cells of the anterior region.
evidence: This is based on analysis of track longevity from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: The tracks of cells in the anterior PS region show mainly angles with the midline between 0° and 45°, indicating limited convergence toward the midline.
source: The tracks of cells in the anterior PS region show mainly angles with the midline between 0° and 45°, indicating limited convergence toward the midline.
evidence: This is based on analysis of track angles from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: Epiblast cells in the posterior half of the PS show angles from 45° to 90° throughout PS regression, suggesting that these cells converge toward the midline to join the PS.
source: In contrast, epiblast cells in the posterior half of the PS show angles from 45° to 90° throughout PS regression, suggesting that these cells converge toward the midline to join the PS (Figure 6C, D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of track angles from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 6C, D and supplementary figures.

claim: Epiblast cells of the anterior PS region show a low VLM compared to the posterior PS.
source: This revealed a low VLM in the anterior PS region compared to the posterior PS.
evidence: This is based on velocity measurements from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Epiblast cells of the anterior PS region show a high VAP, similar to that of the node, suggesting that they follow the node posterior movements.
source: In contrast, epiblast cells of the anterior PS region show a high VAP, similar to that of the node, suggesting that they follow the node posterior movements.
evidence: This is based on velocity measurements from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 6E.

claim: VAP decreases progressively in the LP domain to become minimal in the posterior-most region.
source: VAP decreases progressively in the LP domain to become minimal in the posterior-most region.
evidence: This is based on velocity measurements from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A gradual posterior to anterior increase of fluorescence over time in the mesoderm along the PS was observed, indicating an anteroposterior gradient of cell ingression of epiblastic cells along the PS.
source: We observed a gradual posterior to anterior increase of fluorescence over time in the mesoderm along the PS (Figure 6G, H). In addition, we could fit the different curves of intensity measurements along the anteroposterior axis to a linear curve, indicating an anteroposterior gradient of cell ingression of epiblastic cells along the PS (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is based on ventral imaging of nuclear red labeled embryos and fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 6G, H.

claim: The ingression pattern parallels the distribution of laminin along the PS, which progressively disappears posteriorly, consistent with a more active ingression behavior.
source: This ingression pattern parallels the distribution of laminin along the PS, which progressively disappears posteriorly (Figure 6I), consistent with a more active ingression behavior.
evidence: This is based on laminin immunostaining shown in Figure 6I and comparison with ingression measurements.

claim: The epiblast gradient of convergence speed is coupled to graded cell ingression along the PS anteroposterior axis with minimal ingression in the anterior PS region where NMP cells reside.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrate that the epiblast gradient of convergence speed is coupled to graded cell ingression along the PS anteroposterior axis with minimal ingression in the anterior PS region where NMP cells reside.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the convergence and ingression measurements.

claim: The number of SOX2/T cells gradually increases from stage 4+HH to reach a peak around 30 somites.
source: We noted that the number of SOX2/T cells gradually increases from stage 4+HH to reach a peak around 30 somites (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on quantification of SOX2/T double-positive cells shown in Figure 7A.

claim: During PS regression, a higher number of phospho-histone 3 (pH3)-positive cells relative to the total number of cells (mitotic index) was observed in the anterior region of the PS compared to more posterior ones.
source: During PS regression, we observed a higher number of phospho-histone 3 (pH3)-positive cells relative to the total number of cells (mitotic index) in the anterior region of the PS compared to more posterior ones (Figure 7B, C).
evidence: This is based on pH3 immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 7B, C.

claim: Confocal live imaging of fluorescent H2B-Cherry quail embryos showed more dividing cells in the anterior PS compared to more posterior regions at the same developmental stage.
source: We performed confocal live imaging of fluorescent H2B-Cherry quail embryos and observed more dividing cells in the anterior PS compared to more posterior regions at the same developmental stage (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on live imaging of transgenic quail embryos and quantification shown in Figure 7D.

claim: This confirmed the existence of a higher mitotic index in the anterior region compared to more posterior parts of the PS.
source: This confirmed the existence of a higher mitotic index in the anterior region compared to more posterior parts of the PS (Stern, 1979).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proliferation measurements and reference to previous work.

claim: All the cells tracked in the mid PS region spent from 1 to 3 hr in the PS before ingressing.
source: All the cells tracked in the mid PS region spent from 1 to 3 hr in the PS before ingressing.
evidence: This is based on manual tracking of electroporated cells shown in Figure 7E, F.

claim: Only 35% of the tracked cells in the anterior PS region show fast ingression dynamics (within 1–3 hr), whereas 65% remain in the PS for more than 7 hr.
source: In contrast, only 35% of the tracked cells in the anterior PS region show such fast ingression dynamics (within 1–3 hr), whereas 65% remain in the PS for more than 7 hr (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on manual tracking of electroporated cells and quantification shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The cell cycle time for symmetric divisions where the two daughter cells remain in the epiblast is around 4.5 hr.
source: The cell cycle time for such symmetric divisions is around 4.5 hr in agreement with the number of divisions predicted by the model (Figure 7G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B, Video 6).
evidence: This is based on manual tracking of dividing cells and measurement of inter-division time shown in Figure 7G and supplementary figures.

claim: Symmetric cell divisions were identified where the two daughter cells remain in the epiblast after cell division, consistent with self-renewal of this population.
source: We identified symmetric cell divisions where the two daughter cells remain in the epiblast after cell division, consistent with self-renewal of this population.
evidence: This is based on tracking of dividing cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Other symmetric cell divisions gave rise to two daughter cells entering the mesoderm.
source: Other symmetric cell divisions gave rise to two daughter cells entering the mesoderm (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on tracking of dividing cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Asymmetric cell divisions were observed where one of the daughter cells ingresses after cell division, suggesting a specification of one of the daughter cells to a mesodermal fate.
source: We also observed asymmetric cell divisions where one of the daughter cells ingresses after cell division, thus suggesting a specification of one of the daughter cells to a mesodermal fate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on tracking of dividing cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells in the NMP region exhibit rapid cell divisions together with limited cell ingression, allowing their self-renewal and amplification during formation of the posterior body.
source: Thus, we show that cells in the NMP region exhibit rapid cell divisions together with limited cell ingression, allowing their self-renewal and amplification during formation of the posterior body.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proliferation and ingression measurements.

claim: A faster reduction of the posterior PS domains was observed, with the extraembryonic territory disappearing first, followed by the LP territory whose ingression is completed at the 10-somite stage.
source: We observed a faster reduction of the posterior PS domains, with the extraembryonic territory disappearing first, followed by the LP territory whose ingression is completed at the 10-somite stage (Figure 8A, D; Moreau et al., 2019; Spratt, 1947).
evidence: This is based on tracking of PS territories in time-lapse movies shown in Figure 8A, D and references to previous work.

claim: After the 10-somite stage, most T-positive progenitors of the superficial layer of the tail bud also express SOX2, suggesting that they correspond to the remnant of the epiblast flanking the anterior PS and remain the only axial progenitors left in the tail bud.
source: After this stage, most T-positive progenitors of the superficial layer of the tail bud also express SOX2, suggesting that they correspond to the remnant of the epiblast flanking the anterior PS and remain the only axial progenitors left in the tail bud (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data and tracking of PS territories shown in Figure 8D.

claim: A sequential posterior to anterior exhaustion of the territories of the extraembryonic mesoderm, the lateral plate, and the SOX2-negative PMPs was observed, which results in finally locating the NMP territory in the tail bud.
source: We observe a sequential posterior to anterior exhaustion of the territories of the extraembryonic mesoderm, the lateral plate, and the SOX2-negative PMPs, which results in finally locating the NMP territory in the tail bud (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on tracking of PS territories shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The significant contribution of cells of the SOX2/T territory of the anterior PS to both neural and mesodermal lineages has been missed in previous fate mapping studies of this region in chicken embryos.
source: The significant contribution of cells of the SOX2/T territory of the anterior PS to both neural and mesodermal lineages has been missed in previous fate mapping studies of this region in chicken embryos (Brown and Storey, 2000; Fernández-Garre et al., 2002; Henrique et al., 1997; Iimura et al., 2007; Psychoyos and Stern, 1996; Schoenwolf et al., 1992; Selleck and Stern, 1991).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of the current findings with previous fate mapping studies.

claim: Compared to previous fate mapping studies, the current study analyzed lineage-tracing experiments at significantly later stages after in ovo labeling (stage 17–20HH instead of stage 10–14HH).
source: Compared to these studies, we analyzed our lineage-tracing experiments at significantly later stages after in ovo labeling (stage 17–20HH instead of stage 10–14HH).
evidence: This is a methodological comparison with previous studies.

claim: While fate maps indicate that cells of the anterior PS epiblast initially produce either neural or mesoderm descendants, NMPs can give rise to both lineages but mostly later, in more posterior regions of the body.
source: Thus, while these fate maps indicate that cells of the anterior PS epiblast initially produce either neural or mesoderm descendants, a trend also observed in mouse clones (Tzouanacou et al., 2009), NMPs can give rise to both lineages but mostly later, in more posterior regions of the body.
evidence: This is an interpretation that reconciles the current findings with previous fate mapping studies and reference to mouse clonal analysis.

claim: Recent grafts of the epiblast territory in 6-somite chicken embryos showed that the territory first produces neural and then both mesodermal and neural derivatives, consistent with the current observations.
source: These observations are consistent with recent grafts of the epiblast territory in 6-somite chicken embryos showing that the territory first produces neural and then both mesodermal and neural derivatives (Kawachi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with a recent study that supports the current findings.

claim: Direct identification of bipotential cells with a neural and mesodermal fate has been reported in zebrafish where they segregate during gastrulation and contribute to the most posterior part of the axis.
source: Direct identification of bipotential cells with a neural and mesodermal fate has been reported in zebrafish where they segregate during gastrulation and contribute to the most posterior part of the axis (Attardi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a reference to findings in zebrafish for comparison.

claim: In zebrafish, only monopotent cells were found in the tail bud, while this is not the case in chicken and mouse.
source: In zebrafish, however, only monopotent cells were found in the tail bud (Attardi et al., 2018; Kanki and Ho, 1997), while this is not the case in chicken (this report) and mouse (Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison of findings across species with references to previous work.

claim: The mouse NMP cluster shows expression of the NMP markers T, Sox2, and Nkx1.2.
source: While the mouse NMP cluster shows expression of the NMP markers T, Sox2, and Nkx1.2, only T was identified in the chicken NMP cluster.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Only T was identified in the chicken NMP cluster, while SOX2 and NKX1.2 (SAX1) expression was neither found in the NMP cluster nor in neural tissue.
source: While the mouse NMP cluster shows expression of the NMP markers T, Sox2, and Nkx1.2, only T was identified in the chicken NMP cluster. SOX2 and NKX1.2 (SAX1) expression was neither found in the NMP cluster nor in neural tissue, suggesting a problem with annotation in the chicken genome.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data and suggests a technical limitation.

claim: The difference in SOX2 and NKX1.2 detection between mouse and chicken might reflect a difference in sequencing depth as the chicken dataset was obtained using the inDrops pipeline, whereas most of the mouse data was obtained with the 10X platform.
source: Alternatively, this might reflect a difference in sequencing depth as the chicken dataset was obtained using the inDrops pipeline, whereas most of the mouse data was obtained with the 10X platform.
evidence: This is a speculation about technical differences between datasets.

claim: Using WOT trajectory analysis, no bias for the NMP contribution toward the neural or mesodermal fate was found, which aligns with lineage-tracing data that does not show any preferential enrichment toward a specific fate.
source: We were not able to find any bias for the NMP contribution toward the neural or mesodermal fate. This result aligns with our lineage-tracing data, which does not show any preferential enrichment toward a specific fate in our analysis timeframe.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on WOT analysis and comparison with lineage tracing data.

claim: Genes associated to the NMP trajectory were identified, including previously undescribed ones such as RARG or MNX1 in both the mouse and chicken datasets.
source: Interestingly, we identified genes associated to the NMP trajectory, including previously undescribed ones such as RARG or MNX1 in both the mouse and chicken datasets.
evidence: This is based on WOT trajectory analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Expected transcription factors that are predictive of the fate differentiation toward the neural (PAX6) and PSM lineages (MSGN1) were identified.
source: We also identified expected transcription factors that are predictive of the fate differentiation toward the neural (PAX6) and PSM lineages (MSGN1).
evidence: This is based on WOT trajectory analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: An increase in SOX2/T cell numbers during axis elongation was observed, indicating that these cells can self-renew while giving rise to a progeny in the paraxial mesoderm and in the neural tube.
source: As reported for mouse embryos (Wymeersch et al., 2016; Wymeersch et al., 2019), we observe an increase in SOX2/T cell numbers during axis elongation, indicating that these cells can self-renew while giving rise to a progeny in the paraxial mesoderm and in the neural tube.
evidence: This is based on quantification of SOX2/T cells and reference to previous work in mouse.

claim: Labeling experiments in mouse and chicken embryos have identified a population of epiblast cells in the region of the anterior PS and Hensen's node, which behave as stem cells, giving rise to descendants in the paraxial mesoderm while being able to self-renew.
source: Labeling experiments in mouse and chicken embryos have identified a population of epiblast cells in the region of the anterior PS and Hensen's node, which behave as stem cells, giving rise to descendants in the paraxial mesoderm while being able to self-renew (Cambray and Wilson, 2002; Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Iimura et al., 2007; McGrew et al., 2008; Nicolas et al., 1996; Selleck and Stern, 1991; Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a reference to previous labeling experiments in mouse and chicken.

claim: These stem cells were proposed to contribute mostly to medial somites while lateral somitic cells are derived from more posterior areas of the PS.
source: These cells were proposed to contribute mostly to medial somites while lateral somitic cells are derived from more posterior areas of the PS (Iimura et al., 2007; Selleck and Stern, 1991).
evidence: This is a reference to previous proposals about somite formation.

claim: The anterior SOX2/T territory encompasses Hensen's node and the epiblast adjacent to the anterior PS and approximately corresponds to the territory containing the stem cells fated to give rise to medial somites.
source: The anterior SOX2/T territory encompasses Hensen's node and the epiblast adjacent to the anterior PS and approximately corresponds to the territory containing the stem cells fated to give rise to medial somites.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison of the SOX2/T territory with previous fate mapping studies.

claim: The epiblast territory immediately posterior to the SOX2/T territory does not express SOX2 and exhibits many cells positive for the paraxial mesoderm-specific marker MSGN1.
source: The epiblast territory immediately posterior to the SOX2/T territory does not express SOX2 and exhibits many cells positive for the paraxial mesoderm-specific marker MSGN1 (this study).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data from the current study.

claim: The territory posterior to the SOX2/T territory likely corresponds to the prospective territory of lateral somites, which does not show a stem cell behavior, giving rise to descendants spanning only ~5–7 segments.
source: This territory likely corresponds to the prospective territory of lateral somites, which does not show a stem cell behavior, giving rise to descendants spanning only ~5–7 segments (Iimura et al., 2007; Psychoyos and Stern, 1996).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison with previous fate mapping studies.

claim: The territory posterior to the SOX2/T territory becomes largely exhausted at the end of PS regression, resulting in posterior somites to derive mostly from the NMPs.
source: Our data suggest that this territory becomes largely exhausted at the end of PS regression, resulting in posterior somites to derive mostly from the NMPs (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on tracking of PS territories shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The selective contribution of different PS territories to medial or lateral somitic territories only applies to anterior somites, consistent with observations in chicken and mouse.
source: This is consistent with observations in chicken and mouse demonstrating that the selective contribution of different PS territories to medial or lateral somitic territories only applies to anterior somites (Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Psychoyos and Stern, 1996).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous observations in chicken and mouse.

claim: A parallel posterior to anterior gradient of cell motility of ingressed mesodermal cells has been documented along the regressing PS.
source: A parallel posterior to anterior gradient of cell motility of ingressed mesodermal cells has been documented along the regressing PS (Zamir et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a reference to previous work on mesodermal cell motility.

claim: These graded movements in the mesoderm are largely controlled by a gradient of Fgf8 acting as a repellent on newly ingressed mesodermal cells at this stage.
source: These graded movements in the mesoderm are largely controlled by a gradient of Fgf8 acting as a repellent on newly ingressed mesodermal cells at this stage (Yang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a reference to previous work on Fgf8 signaling.

claim: The cellular dynamics suggests that the movement away from the posterior PS could act as a sink for the epiblastic territories generating these progenitors.
source: This cellular dynamics suggests that the movement away from the posterior PS could act as a sink for the epiblastic territories generating these progenitors.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed cell movements.

claim: These cell movements in the epiblast and the ingressing mesoderm could explain the progressive exhaustion of the PS from its posterior end first described for the extraembryonic territory.
source: These cell movements in the epiblast and the ingressing mesoderm could explain the progressive exhaustion of the PS from its posterior end first described for the extraembryonic territory (Spratt, 1947).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed cell movements and reference to previous work.

claim: Combined with increased proliferation in the NMP region, the sequential exhaustion of PS territories could explain why the SOX2/T territory eventually remains as the major remnant of the PS in the tail bud after PS regression.
source: Combined to an increased proliferation in the NMP region, this could explain why the SOX2/T territory eventually remains as the major remnant of the PS in the tail bud after PS regression.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the proliferation and exhaustion data.

claim: While most of the PS behave as a transit zone for committed progenitors as proposed by Pasteels, its anterior-most region behaves more like a blastema, containing multipotential cells as predicted by Wetzel.
source: Thus, while most of the PS behave as a transit zone for committed progenitors as proposed by Pasteels, 1937, its anterior-most region behaves more like a blastema, containing multipotential cells as predicted by Wetzel (Romanoff, 1960; Wetzel, 1929).
evidence: This is an interpretation that reconciles different historical models with the current findings.

claim: The fact that the tail bud contains multipotent NMPs in addition to monopotent territories such as the precursors of the notochord or the hindgut could explain the long-standing controversy on whether the tail bud functions as a blastema or as a mosaic of committed precursors.
source: The fact that the tail bud contains multipotent NMPs in addition to monopotent territories such as the precursors of the notochord or the hindgut could explain the long-standing controversy on whether the tail bud functions as a blastema or as a mosaic of committed precursors (Catala et al., 1995; Davis and Kirschner, 2000; Gont et al., 1993; Holmdahl, 1925).
evidence: This is an interpretation that addresses a historical controversy with references to previous work.

claim: NMPs can contribute to a single type of derivative (neural or mesodermal) for several segments followed by another type in the next segments, as reported in mouse embryos.
source: Here, we show that NMPs can contribute to a single type of derivative (neural or mesodermal) for several segments followed by another type in the next segments, as reported in mouse embryos (Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on lineage tracing data and reference to previous work in mouse.

claim: The observation that NMPs can contribute to different derivatives in different segments argues for a striking plasticity of NMPs and rules out simple models of asymmetric divisions for the generation of neural and mesodermal descendants.
source: This argues for a striking plasticity of NMPs and rules out simple models of asymmetric divisions for the generation of neural and mesodermal descendants.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lineage tracing data.

claim: Bifated clones that do not contribute to the tail bud were observed, as reported in mouse.
source: Furthermore, as reported in mouse, we also observed bifated clones that do not contribute to the tail bud (Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on lineage tracing data and reference to previous work in mouse.

claim: Plasticity of the NMPs is supported by heterotopic grafts of the NMP epiblast territory into territories fated to become neural or mesodermal, which resulted in the donor cells to adopt the fate of their new territory in chicken or mouse embryos.
source: Plasticity of the NMPs is supported by heterotopic grafts of the NMP epiblast territory into territories fated to become neural or mesodermal, which resulted in the donor cells to adopt the fate of their new territory in chicken or mouse embryos (Garcia-Martinez et al., 1997; McGrew et al., 2008; Wymeersch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a reference to previous grafting experiments that support NMP plasticity.

claim: The results suggest that the NMP population behaves as a unique stem cell population that remains uncommitted toward either lineage, with its descendants acquiring their identity only after entering the territory of the paraxial mesoderm or the neural tube.
source: Our results also show that the transcriptional identity of the NMP population remains largely stable throughout axis formation. This suggests that the NMP population behaves as a unique stem cell population that remains uncommitted toward either lineage, with its descendants acquiring their identity only after entering the territory of the paraxial mesoderm or the neural tube.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the scRNAseq and lineage tracing data.

claim: Such plasticity is supported by the observation that SOX2/T-positive NMP-like cells generated in vitro can be induced to differentiate to either neural or mesodermal cells by changing the culture conditions.
source: Such plasticity is supported by the observation that SOX2/T-positive NMP-like cells generated in vitro can be induced to differentiate to either neural or mesodermal cells by changing the culture conditions (Diaz-Cuadros et al., 2020; Edri et al., 2019a; Edri et al., 2019b; Gouti et al., 2017; Gouti et al., 2014; Henrique et al., 2015; Turner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a reference to previous in vitro studies that support NMP plasticity.

claim: The difficulty to observe NMPs in vivo contrasts with the ease with which NMP-like cells can be obtained in vitro from mouse or human pluripotent stem cells.
source: The difficulty to observe NMPs in vivo contrasts with the ease with which NMP-like cells can be obtained in vitro from mouse or human pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: This is a comparison between in vivo and in vitro observations.

claim: NMPs have been generated in 2D cultures by activation of Wnt signaling at the epiblast-like stage.
source: NMPs have been generated in 2D cultures by activation of Wnt signaling at the epiblast-like stage (Diaz-Cuadros et al., 2020; Edri et al., 2019a; Edri et al., 2019b; Gouti et al., 2017; Gouti et al., 2014; Henrique et al., 2015; Turner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a reference to previous in vitro studies on NMP generation.

claim: Analysis of 3D cultures such as gastruloids induced in vitro from mouse ES cells shows that most of the cells forming these structures belong to the neural tube and paraxial mesoderm lineage, suggesting that they are largely derived from an initial NMP population.
source: Analysis of 3D cultures such as gastruloids induced in vitro from mouse ES cells also shows that most of the cells forming these structures belong to the neural tube and paraxial mesoderm lineage, suggesting that they are largely derived from an initial NMP population (Beccari et al., 2018; Faustino Martins et al., 2020; van den Brink et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a reference to previous studies on gastruloids.

claim: NMP-like cells generated in vitro express both SOX2 and T and single-cell RNA-sequencing demonstrated that they form a very homogeneous population with characteristics similar to the endogenous SOX2/T cells.
source: NMP-like cells generated in vitro express both SOX2 and T and single-cell RNA-sequencing demonstrated that they form a very homogeneous population with characteristics similar to the endogenous SOX2/T cells (Diaz-Cuadros et al., 2020; Gouti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a reference to previous in vitro studies characterizing NMP-like cells.

claim: Comparison of chicken, mouse, and human NMP cells identified by scRNAseq points to a significant level of conservation of the transcriptional signature of this population.
source: Our comparison of chicken, mouse, and human NMP cells identified by scRNAseq points to an significant level of conservation of the transcriptional signature of this population.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of scRNAseq data across species.
